initial_posts.content: I support the Cedarbrook eight-week pilot if the intersections are protected. I currently avoid Main Street because traffic feels unsafe. A protected lane on Main Street could make my commute viable again, and I would value clear intersection treatment during the trial.

I am concerned about losing short-stay parking on Main Street, but I could support the Cedarbrook trial if loading access remains reliable and customer visits are measured during the eight-week pilot. Two signed loading bays are a start; I would like clarity on delivery windows.

Accessible pickup spaces and a clear pedestrian path must remain during the Cedarbrook pilot. A bike lane alone does not answer those needs. I would like to see how accessibility is protected alongside the bike-lane design before the eight weeks begin.

The Cedarbrook bike-lane pilot is reversible. We will publish counts of cyclists, deliveries, customer visits and accessibility complaints before considering any permanent change. The eight-week timeline exists to gather those measurements, not to predetermine an outcome.

event_config.narrative_direction: The four named participants are expected to converge on a conditional-support framing: pilot proceeds with emphasis on intersection protection (Maya), maintained loading and measured visits (Leo), preserved accessibility features (Priya), and reversible measurement-based evaluation with published counts before any permanence decision (Daniel). Opinions should sharpen around measurement design rather than ideological opposition. Upside case: all four align on protected design, clear loading/accessibility provisions, and credible measurement metrics. Downside case: Leo demands stronger delivery guarantees or visit monitoring, Priya flags accessibility gaps, slowing rollout or prompting design revisions. Base case: conditional cooperation across all four with concrete guardrails, no permanence decision and no fabricated data.

scheduled_events.content: Round 1 opens with the four participants restating their positions: Maya (Cyclist) presses for protected intersections, Leo (ShopOwner) raises loading-bay reliability and customer-visit measurement, Priya (AccessibilityAdvocate) flags accessible pickup and pedestrian path, Daniel (TransportPlanner) reaffirms reversibility and published counts. No survey, crash, revenue or permanence data is introduced.
scheduled_events.expected_effect: Locks in the conditional-support framing. Establishes the base case as most likely: cooperation on guardrails with no permanence commitment. Reduces probability of premature polarization.
scheduled_events.title: Pilot design discussion: intersection protection and loading bays

scheduled_events.content: Leo (ShopOwner) asks Daniel (TransportPlanner) for written delivery-window rules at the two signed loading bays, framing it as a condition for not opposing the trial. Daniel indicates windows can be clarified without changing the reversible pilot structure.
scheduled_events.expected_effect: Slight upward pressure on downside case if delivery clarity is not formalized, but base case holds: a procedural clarification, not a redesign. Keeps probability weight on conditional cooperation.
scheduled_events.title: Shop owner requests clearer delivery-window specification

scheduled_events.content: Round 2: Daniel (TransportPlanner) confirms the published counts will cover cyclists, deliveries, customer visits and accessibility complaints, gathered over the eight weeks. Maya (Cyclist) accepts the measurement-based approach if intersection protection is in place. Leo (ShopOwner) accepts conditional on reliable loading and the customer-visit count being shared. Priya (AccessibilityAdvocate) accepts conditional on accessible pickup and pedestrian path being preserved. No decision is made on permanence.
scheduled_events.expected_effect: Strengthens base case. All four participants move from conditional concern to conditional acceptance. Upside case probability rises modestly if the agreed measurement scope is publicly readable and not later expanded. Downside case probability recedes.
scheduled_events.title: Measurement scope agreed, no permanence decision

scheduled_events.content: Priya (AccessibilityAdvocate) raises a specific design question: width and obstruction rules for the pedestrian path adjacent to the bike lane. Maya (Cyclist) supports adequate pedestrian width. Daniel (TransportPlanner) notes this can be addressed within the reversible pilot design without changing scope.
scheduled_events.expected_effect: Mild downside pressure if the pedestrian-path detail is left vague, but the TransportPlanner response keeps it inside base case. Reinforces that the pilot remains reversible and scope-bounded; no permanence drift.
scheduled_events.title: Accessibility advocate emphasizes pedestrian-path design detail
